sections: The viewer shows a tickwave recording. Each channel has a row, all on one time axis. A digital channel is drawn from its edges, and an analog channel from its samples. The same view opens on the Open page and wherever a page cites a recording, as tickwave's main page does.

Give the Open page a recording's address, and its sidecar's if it has one. The page's address then names both, as ?src= and ?annotations=, so a link to it opens the same recording. With ?annotation= as well, it opens at that annotation. ?window= gives a span to show, as two tick counts, such as ?window=377113809+377124212. A zoomed-in figure links to the span it shows this way. A recording on another site opens only if that site lets other sites read its files: its server has to answer with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header (CORS). Or open files from this computer: a .tickwave recording, with its sidecar's .toml and .jsonl files if it has them. They stay in your browser, and nothing is uploaded. A link can't share them. A capture converts on the Open page first, where its channels can be moved and trimmed: the converter's doc says how. There, another capture or recording can join the one shown, to merge them on one time axis, each recording lined up with the others by hand. A reading in a merged recording keeps to the tick of the recording its channel came from, and a span between two recordings' channels to the coarser of their ticks. A .zip of these files opens as the files would. The folders inside it don't matter, but two files with one name do: the page refuses those, since either could be the one meant. With several recordings in it, the page lists them to open one at a time, each with the sidecar named after it. The page reads files a zip stores as they are or deflated, as common zip tools write them. Under the view, the recording's details give its title, length and channels, the time one tick stands for, its size, what it was converted from, and its content id. A recording's sidecar can store how a view of it starts: which channels it shows, in what order, the span it opens at, and the trace's colour. The view starts that way wherever the page says nothing else. Bundled into the recording, the sidecar goes with it, so a recording downloaded from a page opens here as the page showed it. A view on a page may offer Download beside Open, and Annotations where it has a sidecar. Download saves the recording as the page serves it, its bundled sidecar with it. Annotations opens a list of the sidecar's files: the hand-written file, then each file it includes. Each link saves one file under its own name. A recording can hold a channel this viewer can't read, such as one a newer tool wrote in a way this version doesn't know. Its row keeps its place and says it is unavailable, and nothing of it is drawn. Annotations that name it are left out, and a note under the view says which.

A capture attached to a GitHub issue or discussion opens in any browser, a phone's included, with nothing to install. GitHub takes attachments of up to 25 MB, in a list of formats that leaves out .tickwave. So zip the recording first, with its sidecar's files if it has them. A capture to convert can go in the zip instead: a Saleae export's folder, or a .sr or .vcd file. GitHub doesn't let other sites read its attachments, so the Open page can't fetch one. Give the attachment's address to the page as a recording's address, and the page shows two steps instead: download the zip, then choose it. The page's address is then the link to post beside the attachment. It is the Open page with ?src= and the attachment's address, such as open.html?src=https://github.com/user-attachments/files/123/capture.zip. A reader who follows the link downloads the zip and chooses it on the page; on a phone, from its downloads. If the browser unzips the download itself, choose the .tickwave file inside. The page takes only GitHub's own attachment addresses this way. An attachment in a private repository needs a GitHub sign-in to download, so share captures in a public one.

Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and turn the wheel to zoom about the pointer, or pinch on a trackpad or a touch screen. The plain wheel scrolls the page. Drag, swipe sideways or hold Shift with the wheel to move along the capture. A zoom step eases into place over about 150 ms. Where the system is set to reduce motion, it jumps there instead, and so it does where the view takes longer to draw than a frame at 60 Hz. With the view focused, the left and right arrow keys move it, an eighth of the span shown at a time, or half with Shift. Each move glides into place as a zoom step does, and a key held down glides on. The up and down arrows, or plus and minus, zoom in and out. Home and the Fit button show the whole capture, and every analog channel's whole range. Escape clears the cursors and the selection. A key held with Alt, Ctrl or Cmd is left to the browser, so Alt with an arrow still goes back or forward.

Point at a row to read it there. An analog channel gives the sample's value, or the smallest and largest value where one pixel covers several samples. On a digital channel, two spans mark the pulse under the pointer: its width, between its edges, and its period, to the next edge the same way. A label gives the pulse's duty, its frequency and 1/width. That is the width as a rate: one UART bit's gives the baud rate. Once the row is tall enough, the width and the period sit on their spans; until then the label gives them too. The label sits on the edge of the rows away from the row you point at, so it never covers the wave you are reading. Where one pixel holds several edges, the label gives how many there are in the time the pixel covers, and how much of that time the channel was high, then asks you to zoom in. Zoomed far out, the view reads these from the recording's overview. It keeps each stretch's edge count to within about 19 %, and its time high to the nearest fourteenth. There the label gives the range those allow, such as "1,024 to 1,217 edges" and "high 32.1 to 39.3 %". A stretch with edges and almost no time high reads "high under 3.6 %": the edges show the channel did go high. A long pulse can end far past what the view has read, as on a quiet line seen close up. The label then says it is measuring. Keep the pointer within the pulse and it goes on; once measured, the pulse reads at once anywhere along it. Where the instrument lost data, the row is shaded: where a digital channel's level was not known, and where an analog channel lost samples, between two runs of samples, before its first or after its last. The trace breaks there. Where the instrument only paused, the trace breaks and nothing is shaded.

Zoomed out, a digital channel's edges come closer together than a pixel. There the row shades the band between its two levels instead of drawing each edge. How dark the shade is says how fast the channel switches, in edges a second. The scale is the same at every zoom and in every recording: faint at one edge a second or fewer, 60 % of the line's ink at 100 million and above, and darker by the same step for every tenfold rise between. Two captures of the same activity look alike side by side. Even the busiest band stays lighter than the line, so a crowded stretch reads as a fill. Each level's line shades with the band, by the share of the time the channel spent at that level over the few pixels around it. The level it spent most time at takes the band's shade; the other takes a part of it, in proportion. An even clock's two lines both take the band's shade; a line high three quarters of the time has its high line at the band's shade and its low line at a third of it. Wherever the stretch holds an edge, the fainter line shows at least a fifth of the band's shade, so a rare excursion stays visible. Outside a busy stretch a held level's line is solid, so it steps from solid to the band's shade where a stretch begins. A short pause between two busy stretches keeps its gap, and its line takes the band's shade. An edge that stands apart is a line across the band. So is a short pulse or burst that stands apart: edges too close together to show apart, spanning too little to fill a stretch, draw as one line at their middle, whatever pixel they fall in. A flag raised for a few microseconds in an hour reads as a solid line at every zoom, and so does each of several flags raised close together. Where other edges come near each other without crowding into one pixel, each line fades towards the shade a stretch of them would take, so neighbouring edges and a crowded stretch read alike. Zoomed in on a burst far busier than the rest of a long capture, the row goes on shading it until the view is narrow enough to hold its edges.

Drag a row's lower edge in the names column to make the row taller or shorter. With that edge focused, the up and down arrows do it too, with Shift for bigger steps. Home and End give the row its least and greatest height, and Enter or a double click its default.

An analog row's scale, the values at its left, zooms and moves on its own. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and turn the wheel over the scale to zoom its values about the pointer, or pinch it with two fingers on a touch screen. Drag the scale up or down to move its values. A double click fits it to the values in view. It zooms in no further than four steps of the instrument's resolution. The view waits for every analog channel's overall range before it draws, so the scales and the channel names beside them are in place from the first frame. A recording gives the range with the first data the view loads. In a merge preview at the fastest recording's rate, a channel whose ticks don't fall on whole ticks of that rate has no range at first: its row shows the channel's name alone until the view has shown all of the channel, and then its scale. Once the values are zoomed in, a drag over the row's traces with a mouse or a pen moves them up and down as well as along the capture. On a touch screen, a finger moving up or down there scrolls the page, so move the values with a finger on the scale. With the scale focused, the up and down arrows move it, with Shift for bigger steps, and plus and minus zoom it. Enter fits it to the values in view, and Home shows its whole range.

A click places cursor A, and the next click cursor B. With the view focused, Enter places them at the middle of the view. A cursor snaps to an edge within a few pixels on the row clicked. The readout under the view gives both cursors' times and the interval between them. It gives each analog channel's value at each cursor, and each digital channel's pulse at cursor A. Drag along the time axis to select a span. The readout gives its length and counts each channel's edges in it. For one channel it measures the clock: how many periods there are, their least, median and greatest, and the running clock. That is the clock's rate and period with the pauses left out. A span with more than 2,097,152 different periods, far more than a clock has, gets no median, and its running clock is the mean of every period, the pauses with them. The readout says so.

A recording can come with annotations, from its sidecar: named spans and points, shown above the channels. Click an annotation's label to show its span. The menu beside the zoom buttons steps through one kind of annotation, such as every WAIT a target answered. It starts at the kind of the annotation the view opened at, or else the kind of the sidecar's first one. An annotation can paint its channels in a role, such as who drives a line: the probe, the target, or neither. The line takes the role's colour, weight and dash over the annotation's span. The sidecar declares its roles, each with a label and a look of its own, which a page can restyle. A key beside the zoom buttons lists every role, as its lines are drawn.

On the Open page, Edit annotations opens the sidecar's hand-written file for editing. A recording without a sidecar starts one. To add an annotation, drag along the time axis to select a span, or click to place cursor A, and press New annotation. It covers the selection, or it is a point at cursor A. Give it a label, and its id follows the label until you type one of your own. A page cites it by its id. Choose an annotation from the list under the form, or click its label in the view, to change it or delete it. The arrows beside it move it up or down the list. Order matters: the view steps through the kind of the first annotation. A decoder writes its own annotations, and rewrites them each time it runs, so they can be read here but not changed. Name it adds a hand-written annotation that refers to one, for a page to cite by a name of your own. It takes the decoder's span and channels, and any field you leave empty. Paint offers the roles the sidecar declares. A paint must name one of them: declare a new role in the sidecar's file first. A change that would break one of the sidecar's checks is refused, and the form says why. The editor changes only what you change: the file keeps its comments, its order and its layout. On this site, Download the sidecar saves the file to your downloads. When tickwave open shows the recording, Save the sidecar writes it back beside the recording instead.

tickwave is a command-line program. It converts captures into tickwave recordings, describes a recording, opens one in your browser, checks one against the capture it came from, checks and bundles a recording's sidecar of annotations, finishes a recording that was cut off before its end, and re-cuts a recording that a recorder flushed often into blocks of the usual size. The Open page runs the same conversion in a browser.

You need a current Rust toolchain, a C compiler and a checkout of tickwave's repository. From the repository's root: cargo build --release -p escapement-tickwave-cli The program is then target/release/tickwave. tickwave help, and --help after any command, list its options. To open recordings in your browser, the program carries the viewer. Build the web pages first, as the repository's README says, then: cargo build --release -p escapement-tickwave-cli --features viewer Without the viewer, tickwave open and --open refuse, and say how to build it.

tickwave convert reads three kinds of capture: saleae: Saleae Logic 2's binary export, version 0 or 1, a directory with one file a channel. sigrok: a sigrok session file (.sr), as PulseView, sigrok-cli and verge write them. vcd: a value change dump (.vcd). It takes one-bit signals and lists the rest as skipped. The converter doesn't read Logic 2's own .sal files, because Saleae doesn't document that format and may change it. Export the capture from Logic 2 first: click Options at the bottom right, then Export Raw Data, and choose the binary format. The converter writes the recording beside its destination first. Then it decodes what it wrote and compares it with the capture, edge by edge and sample by sample. Only a recording that matches takes its place, and if they differ, nothing is left behind. Every edge in a recording lies on a whole tick from the capture's start, and one tick is the source's resolution. A Saleae export's times become ticks by round((t − begin) × rate). The converter refuses an export with an edge more than 0.01 of a tick off that grid, rather than move it. An analog file whose begin sits off that grid keeps the offset as its samples' phase, to a thousandth of a sample, so each sample keeps its place between two ticks. The converter refuses an analog file that begins before the digital channels.

Name each channel you want with --channel, as the export's file name without .bin, then the channel's name. Channels you don't name stay out. tickwave convert saleae identify-swd/ --channel digital_3_0=SWCLK --channel digital_3_1=SWDIO \ --title identify-swd -o identify-swd.tickwave It reports the file it wrote, its size, its blocks and its content id: identify-swd.tickwave: 0.00 MB, 2 blocks, blake3:63773d56fb3420735c864932f8d2441acd6f31a51b557e073bf27755a0534697 in 0.0 s Logic 8, Logic Pro 8 and Logic Pro 16 write version 0 of the export, and its digital files don't record the sample rate. If you name an analog channel, the converter takes the rate its file records. Otherwise it infers the rate from the edges of every digital file in the export, named or not. It takes the lowest rate that divides 1 GHz and puts every edge on its grid, each on a tick of its own. With many edges, that is the capture's rate. With only a few, it can come out lower, and the recording then claims coarser timing than the capture had, never finer. An export with no edges has no rate to infer. Give the rate with --rate, in hertz with an optional k, M or G, such as --rate 50M. The converter refuses a rate that puts an edge off its grid. It can't catch a rate higher than the capture's, though: the recording would then claim finer timing than the capture had. The recording says whether its rate was inferred or given.

tickwave convert sigrok session.sr -o session.tickwave Without --channel, every enabled channel goes in under its own name. With it, only the channels you name go in, as --channel <probe name>=<name>.
tickwave convert vcd dump.vcd -o dump.tickwave --channel top.dut.clk=CLK Without --channel, every one-bit signal goes in, named by its scope path. With it, name each signal by its scope path.

Where a capture's analog values are the instrument's integer codes, the converter stores the codes and the scale that turns them back into values. It checks that every sample comes back exactly first. Otherwise it stores the values as 32-bit floats, and --no-codes asks for floats anyway. A readout shows a coded value to the digit one code step carries. If the source doesn't state a channel's unit, give it with --unit <name>=<unit>, such as --unit A0=V.

--offset <name>=<time> moves a channel along the time axis, later when the time is positive: --offset SWDIO=-40ns moves SWDIO 40 ns earlier. It corrects a known delay in a channel's path, such as a longer probe lead. The time has to be a whole number of the capture's ticks. --keep <name>=<from>..<to> keeps only that part of a channel, in the capture's time before any move: --keep SWCLK=1.2ms..9.8ms. Leave out either end to keep from the channel's start or to its end. <name> is the name the channel takes in the recording, and a time is ticks or a decimal with a unit, as a sidecar writes it. The recording says how far each channel was moved and, for every channel, where it holds the capture's data, so neither a move nor a cut is taken for what the instrument recorded. A recording with a channel moved or trimmed starts where its earliest kept data does. An analog channel's cut moves forward to the next sample that keeps every sample on its tick.

Option Does -o, --output <file> where to write the recording --title <text> the recording's title, which a view shows; without one, a view shows the file's name --meta <key>=<value> free metadata, such as --meta probe=verge, as often as you like --offset <name>=<time> move a channel, later when the time is positive (above) --keep <name>=<from>..<to> keep only that part of a channel (above) --level <n> the zstd compression level, 19 by default --block-kib <n> how much decoded data each of a channel's blocks aims to hold, 1024 KiB by default and at most 65,536 --open open the recording in your browser once it's written, as tickwave open does A block holds one channel's edges or samples over one stretch of time, and it is the smallest piece of a channel's data a viewer fetches. Smaller blocks mean less waiting for a narrow view of a long capture, and a larger file. Every command that reads a recording takes --max-decoded-mib <n>: the most it decodes from one block, 64 MiB by default. A recording that needs more is refused, as a page's viewer refuses it unless the page sets a larger limit. A block at the largest --block-kib stays under the default.

The Open page converts a capture without installing anything. Choose a Saleae export's folder, or a .sr or .vcd file, or a .zip holding one, or drop it on the page. It converts at once, every channel under the capture's own name, and shows it in a view. Under the view, the page lists the capture's channels, with the options a command line takes: the channels to take and their names, units, a title, metadata, the zstd level, the block size, --no-codes, and for a version 0 Saleae export, --rate. Leave the rate empty to infer it, as the command line does without --rate. In the view, a grip at the left of each row's name moves its channel. Drag it sideways to move the channel in time, as --offset does, or up or down to change its row. Zoomed in far enough to show edges, a channel dragged to within a few pixels of another row's edge puts its own nearest edge on it; hold Alt to move it freely. The bars at the ends of a channel's data trim it, as --keep does, and the part left out fades. Trim every channel to the selection keeps the part of each channel you selected. With a grip or a bar focused, the arrow keys move it. The list shows each channel's move and trim, and takes them typed too, as times such as -40 ns. A move takes the channel's trim with it, so moving and trimming can come in either order. The view always shows all of the capture, so a trim can be undone. Save keeps the recording. With nothing changed, that is the capture as converted. Otherwise Save converts the capture again with the list's settings first. The recording saved then opens, and its annotations can be edited. Shape again goes back to the capture, with the settings as they were. For a Saleae export, it first checks that every edge sits on the sample grid, in order. Then it goes through the capture twice: once to look for exact integer codes in each analog channel, and once to encode. The page runs the converter's own code, compiled to WebAssembly, so the same capture and settings give the same file, byte for byte. It stores channels in the order it lists them, which for a Saleae export is by file name, numbers in order, until you move one. A command line that names the same channels in that order, with the same moves and trims, makes the same file. Under the view, Add a capture or recording takes another to merge with the one shown, as tickwave merge does. Drop it on the view, or choose it: a .tickwave recording with its sidecar's files, a capture, which converts whole first, or a .zip of either. The view then shows them all on one time axis, each recording's rows under its name. Drag the grip by a recording's name sideways to move the whole recording in time, as --align does, and line it up with the others. An edge of it lands on another recording's edge within a few pixels; hold Alt to move it freely. The list gives each recording a head with its alignment, which takes a time typed too, and Remove. A channel's own grip and bars work as for one capture. Save merges the recordings with the list's settings and opens the result. The capture stays in the browser. The page reads a Saleae export a slice at a time, so the export can be larger than the 4 GiB WebAssembly gives the converter. A sigrok or VCD file is read whole, and the recording is built in memory, so these have to fit. The page converts on one thread, where the command line uses every core, so a large capture takes longer.

tickwave merge analyser.tickwave probe.tickwave -o both.tickwave This puts several recordings on one time axis, such as a logic analyser's beside a probe's own stream from the same target. A capture goes through tickwave convert first. Every channel of every recording goes in, in order, under its own name. A channel whose name an earlier recording took is named after its file as well: probe/CLK. The merged recording ticks at the least common multiple of the recordings' tick rates: 500 MHz and 96 MHz merge at 12 GHz, a tick of 83 ps. Where that rate would need a number past 2^53, it ticks at the fastest recording's rate instead. Each channel keeps its own instrument's ticks, and the merged recording states where each instrument's ticks lie on its time axis. Nothing is resampled: every edge and sample keeps its time. A reading still keeps to the tick of the recording it reads, so it never shows more digits than that recording carries. The recordings share no clock: none of the captures tickwave reads records the time of day it started. So each recording starts at the merged recording's start. --align <n>=<time> moves recording n, counting from 1, later when the time is positive, to line it up with the others, on an edge both instruments saw, say. The time is a decimal with a unit, or a whole number of the merged recording's ticks. Those ticks are at the merged rate the merge picks, so a time with a unit says the same thing whichever rate that is. The merged recording states an alignment as a claim, as it does a move. Instruments' clocks drift apart. At 20 ppm, an alignment by one edge stays within one tick of a 96 MHz clock for about half a millisecond either side of the edge, and within 10 µs for about half a second. --stretch <n>=<ratio> lengthens recording n's ticks to make up for it, as a ratio such as 1001/1000 or a change such as +20ppm. A stretch above 1 says the recording's clock ran slow. The merged recording states the stretch on the recording's sources, as a claim. What a stretch leaves is the clocks' wander. Two marks give both at once: --align <n>=<x>@<y>,<x>@<y>. Each mark is an event both instruments saw, x its time in recording n's own time and y its time on the merged recording's axis, both with a unit. For a recording left unaligned, the axis time is that recording's own time. The first mark gives the alignment, and the time between the two gives the stretch. --align 2=1s@1.0016s,9s@9.0024s puts the probe's own 1 s at 1.0016 s and its 9 s at 9.0024 s: a stretch of 1.0001, and its tick 0 1.5 ms in. The stretch is out by each mark's error over the time between them, so take the marks far apart. The merge takes the simplest ratio within that error, with each x good to one tick of recording n's coarsest instrument and each y to one merged tick. A mark has to be an event the instruments can't confuse with another. A periodic signal, such as a 100 Hz marker, lines up equally well at every whole number of its periods: an alignment on one of its edges can be off by a period, and nothing in the recording says so. Align on an aperiodic mark, such as a burst, a reset or a single pulse, and use the periodic signal to measure the drift. Option Does --channel <n>:<name>[=<new>] take channel <name> of recording n, named <new> if given. A recording with no --channel gives every channel --align <n>=<time> move recording n, later when the time is positive --align <n>=<x>@<y>,<x>@<y> place recording n by two marks, which give its alignment and its stretch --stretch <n>=<ratio> lengthen recording n's ticks by a ratio a/b or a change such as +20ppm --offset <name>=<time> move a channel, later when the time is positive, by a whole number of its own instrument's ticks --keep <name>=<from>..<to> keep only that part of a channel, in its own recording's time before any move --unit <name>=<unit> an analog channel's unit <name> is the name the channel takes in the merged recording. -o, --title, --meta, --level, --block-kib and --open work as they do for a conversion. Each recording's own title and metadata stay with its sources, where tickwave info and the Open page's details list them. A recording's generated annotations come with it, from its decoders' files, bundled or in a sidecar beside it. Their times move with the recording, and ANNOTATIONS.md says how their names follow the merge's. Annotations written by hand don't come, since their times are the recording's own, and merge says how many it left out. A derived channel, such as power from a current and a voltage, comes while both its channels do, moved and trimmed alike. A channel's move is in its own instrument's ticks, since that is where its edges and samples sit: a whole number of them, or a time with a unit within a hundredth of one. tickwave verify checks a merged recording against the recordings it merged. It goes by what the merged recording states, not by the options it was given.

tickwave info identify-swd.tickwave identify-swd 0.523583100 s at 1000000000/1 ticks a second, 2 channels, blake3:63773d56fb3420735c864932f8d2441acd6f31a51b557e073bf27755a0534697 source 0: saleae-binary-1 at 1000000000/1 ticks a second, its tick 0 at 0: digital_3_0.bin, digital_3_1.bin SWCLK digital, 15286 edges, starts 1, known to 0.523583070 s (digital_3_0) SWDIO digital, 1874 edges, starts 1, known to 0.523583100 s (digital_3_1) 0.005 MB: footer 867 bytes, 2 blocks of 1424-1727 bytes, median 1727 SWCLK overview strip at 2^21 SWDIO overview strip at 2^24 Times are in seconds to one tick, here a nanosecond: never more digits than the recording carries. Each channel has an overview of its own: levels of buckets of 2^n ticks, which a view draws from when it is zoomed out, from finer ones in the file to the strip in the footer. --json prints the header and the block statistics as JSON, for a script. info reads the recording's footer, at its end, and its index a page at a time, so it holds little however large the recording. For a merged recording, info lists each instrument's source, with how many of the merged recording's ticks one of its ticks lasts and any stretch. Where two instruments may have recorded the same periodic signal, such as a marker line, it says that --drift measures the drift between their clocks. tickwave info --drift decodes the whole recording for it. Here an analyser at 1 GHz and a probe at 100 MHz both recorded a 10 ms marker, and the probe's clock ran 1,000 ppm fast, so it measured each period as 10.01 ms: tickwave info --drift both.tickwave 9.029020000 s at 1000000000/1 ticks a second, 2 channels, blake3:e2e5f04029d12cbef8ed7a63f6bee934e2492c79266ca42adf1a4f2bb4b13c78 source 0: vcd at 1000000000/1 ticks a second, its tick 0 at 0: analyser.vcd source 1: vcd at 100000000/1 ticks a second (10 of the recording's ticks each), its tick 0 at 0: probe.vcd analyser.MARK digital, 1800 edges, starts 0, known to 9.020000000 s (analyser.MARK, source 0) probe.MARK digital, 1800 edges, starts 0, known to 9.029020000 s (probe.MARK, source 1) 0.002 MB: footer 1033 bytes, 2 blocks of 46-76 bytes, median 76 analyser.MARK overview strip at 2^28 probe.MARK overview strip at 2^28 drift: analyser.MARK (source 0) against probe.MARK (source 1): +1000.0 ± 0.0 ppm, the stretch source 0 would take to tick as source 1 does; periods 10.000000 ms and 10.010000 ms over 900 and 900 rises, 0.6 µs and 1.7 µs rms off a straight line It fits each such channel's rising edges to a line. A missed pulse counts as a period with no rise in it, not as one period twice as long. It compares two channels from different instruments whose periods agree within 1 %, and reads only channels of at most 2^20 edges. Their periods' ratio is the drift, as the stretch that would make the first instrument tick as the second does. A recording already stretched shows what the stretch leaves. The rms is each channel's wander about its line.

tickwave open identify-swd.tickwave identify-swd.tickwave: with its sidecar identify-swd.annotations.toml, 695 annotations http://127.0.0.1:38343/open.html?src=bc6452795da2010a0ba21af9322bc366/identify-swd.tickwave&annotations=bc6452795da2010a0ba21af9322bc366/identify-swd.annotations.toml&save=bc6452795da2010a0ba21af9322bc366/identify-swd.annotations.toml&local serving the viewer until Ctrl-C This shows the recording in your browser, on the Open page, with its sidecar's annotations. A page can't read a file from your disk, so tickwave open serves the recording and the viewer itself. It serves them to your own computer only, at 127.0.0.1, and from your disk it serves only the recording, its sidecar and the files the sidecar includes. The viewer reads the recording as you move through it, so it keeps serving until you stop it with Ctrl-C. It takes the sidecar beside the recording by its name: identify-swd.annotations.toml for identify-swd.tickwave. --annotations <file> names another. It checks the sidecar first and lists any problems, and the viewer then shows the recording without its annotations. A recording cut off before its end is refused, and tickwave repair finishes it. It prints the viewer's address and starts your browser on it. --no-browser only prints the address, for a browser you start yourself. --port <n> serves on that port, where otherwise the system chooses one. The page can edit the sidecar's annotations and save the file back beside the recording. A recording with no sidecar gets one on the first save: identify-swd.annotations.toml for identify-swd.tickwave. The page won't save over a sidecar that changed on disk after the page read it, or over one with problems. A conversion opens its recording the same way with --open, once the recording is written. --port and --no-browser go with it: tickwave convert sigrok capture.sr -o capture.tickwave --open
Checking a recording against its capture

tickwave verify identify-swd.tickwave --against identify-swd/ It decodes the recording and compares it with the capture again, edge by edge and sample by sample, and says whether they match: identify-swd.tickwave: matches identify-swd/ For a Saleae export, --against takes its directory. A recording from a version 0 export is checked at the rate it was made at. A recording with a channel moved or trimmed is checked through its moves and cuts, as the recording states them. A merged recording takes --against once for each recording merged into it, in the merge's order. Each is the recording's capture, or the .tickwave recording itself where there is no capture to import, such as a probe's own stream: tickwave verify both.tickwave --against analyser/ --against probe.tickwave It first checks that each one's sources are the ones the merged recording names in that place, and says so if two are swapped. Once the recording matches, it reports the drift between its instruments, as info --drift does.

A recording's annotations live beside it, in a sidecar: one hand-written TOML file, and the JSON Lines files of any programs that generated annotations. The sidecar describes them. tickwave annotations check checks a sidecar against its recording: its ids, its refs, its included files, its channels, its times and the recording id it names. tickwave annotations check identify-swd.tickwave identify-swd.annotations.toml identify-swd.annotations.toml: 695 annotations, 8 hand-written and 687 generated, all check It reads the included files from beside the TOML file, and refuses an included name with a directory in it. If it finds a problem, it lists every one and exits with a non-zero status, so a page's build stops instead of publishing a broken reference: identify-swd.annotations.toml: annotation 1: ref "swd/wait/1" does not resolve Error: 1 problem --json prints the annotations as resolved: times in ticks, refs followed, in the sidecar's order.
Bundling a sidecar into its recording

tickwave bundle identify-swd.tickwave identify-swd.annotations.toml -o identify-swd.bundle.tickwave This writes a copy of the recording with the sidecar's files inside, so one file carries both. It checks the sidecar first. The copy's content id is the recording's: a bundle holds the same capture. A view of a bundled recording shows its annotations when the page names no sidecar.

A recorder writes a recording as it captures, and the file ends with an index of what it holds. A crash, a power cut or a full disk can stop the file before its index, and a viewer then can't open it. tickwave repair finishes such a file: tickwave repair identify-swd.cut.tickwave -o identify-swd.tickwave identify-swd.tickwave: 2929 of 3000 bytes kept, 8 blocks to 0.388970979 s, blake3:3a720b983b1a833de4c025cc9565f15ab5c5c8fa7cf2d7b02dec3902525da876 A recorder that flushes notes, after each flush, the time up to which every channel's data is in the file. Where the file holds such a note, repair keeps every channel to the latest one. Otherwise it keeps each channel's blocks up to its last whole one, and the capture ends where the latest of those ends. Either way what came after was lost with the rest of the file. It then writes the index and the footer, and writes the copy to -o. If the recorder generated annotations, each generator's file goes beside the copy, as <name>.<generator>.jsonl. A finished recording is refused, since there is nothing to repair. So is one with a channel moved or trimmed: convert it again from its capture. Now and then a recording can't be finished as it stands: a loss the recorder was reporting when it stopped leaves a record that a finished file can't hold. Repair then re-cuts the recording instead, as tickwave recut does below, and says so. The copy holds the same content either way.

A recorder that flushes often, as a live capture does so that a crash loses little, closes each channel's block at every flush. At a low data rate those blocks are small, and each costs the same few dozen bytes of framing and index, so the file comes out larger than its data. tickwave recut writes it again with blocks of the usual size. The repository's web/fixtures/energy.tickwave is laid out this way: a synthetic recording of five channels over 30 ms, its current and voltage in six short blocks each, as a recorder flushing every 5 ms leaves them: tickwave recut energy.tickwave -o energy.recut.tickwave energy.recut.tickwave: 0.01 MB from 0.02 MB, 5 blocks, blake3:d9a38a24d16a4cdb984ed2a901f89973b02a8c44d80cf3a5deed33b489148326 in 0.0 s tickwave info counts 24 blocks of 13 to 360 bytes in the original and 5 of 21 to 530 bytes in the copy, 18 KB against 14 KB. The copy holds the same content, with the same content id, and is checked before it is written. --block-kib and --level work as they do for a conversion. A recording cut off before its end is finished as repair would finish it, and each annotation generator's file goes beside the copy.

tickwave puts a capture into a web page with three custom elements. <tickwave-view> shows a whole recording. <tickwave-inset> shows one annotated stretch of it, magnified. <tickwave-ref> turns a phrase in the text into a reference: pointing at it opens an inset beside the text. A fourth, <tickwave-chart>, in a module of its own, draws measurements against a setting. None of them answers a key held with Alt, Ctrl or Cmd: those are the browser's, such as Alt with an arrow to go back or forward.

Include one module, and the three elements are defined: tickwave.js reads recordings through a decoder in a worker. The first time a page needs a recording, it loads tickwave-worker.js and tickwave.wasm from beside itself, so keep the three files together. They can be on another site, such as a release's directory on tickwave's site. That site has to send them with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, as GitHub Pages does. The worker then starts from a small script the page makes, which imports tickwave-worker.js from that site. A page opened from disk can load them from a site this way, and its recordings too, by their full URLs. A page with a Content-Security-Policy has to allow 'unsafe-inline' in style-src, for the styles in the elements' shadow roots. The decoder needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval' in script-src of the policy its worker runs under. On the files' own site, that is the policy sent with tickwave-worker.js, if there is one. When the files are on another site, it is the page's policy, which then also has to allow blob: in worker-src, and that site in connect-src. Recordings are fetched by byte range: the footer first, then only the channels and the span a view shows. A server that ignores ranges still works, as long as it sends the whole file. A recording on another site needs that site to send Access-Control-Allow-Origin, as GitHub Pages does. The decoder then asks for the whole file and stops the read once the answer gives the file's size. So a recording larger than the first read, 32 KiB by default, takes one more request to open. A page that shows a closed view can write the view's title and facts into it. The view then lays out before tickwave.js has loaded, and keeps its height once it has: SWD reads 524 ms; 2 channels: SWCLK, SWDIO; 4.7 KiB tickwave.css lays out a view that is not defined yet the way the view lays out its summary, from the two spans, with an empty cell where the button goes, and where the download links go too on a view with download. Without scripts, that is what the reader sees. Put nothing else inside the view. The sheet's rules carry no specificity, so any rule of the page's wins. So leave the view's display alone: the sheet sets its own.

A whole recording. Closed, it shows the recording's title and, under it, the recording's length to three significant figures, its channels and its size, with an Open button beside them. A view of some of the channels names those out of the recording's, "2 of 3 channels: TCKC, TMSC", and gives the length they span. Once it scrolls into view, it fetches the recording's footer and, where the page names no channels, the stored view a sidecar or a bundle may give; nothing else. Open, all of that stays, and the button reads Close. Below it come the time axis, one row a channel, the annotations above the rows, and a readout under the rows. The button keeps the focus, and names its recording to a screen reader. A page can write the title and the facts itself, as spans with slot="title" and slot="facts" (see Loading). The view shows the page's text in place of its own. Once the footer is in, it compares the two, taking any run of spaces as one, and warns in the console of each that differs. Where the page names no channels and the recording has a sidecar, named or bundled, the facts count the channels its stored view names. So the view reads that first, and only then fills in its own facts, compares and sends its summary. A sidecar that doesn't read leaves the facts on every channel. summary and the tickwave-summary event say that it has compared, so a page's check can tell a match from a view whose footer never came. Attribute Means src the recording's URL annotations its sidecar's TOML file. Without it, a recording with a bundled sidecar shows that channels the channels to show, by name, in order. Without it, those the sidecar's stored view names (ANNOTATIONS.md, "The stored view"), or else all of them. The view then goes as far as the furthest of them ends window what an open view shows first: two times ("317.8 ms 318.0 ms"), or an annotation's id. Without it, the stored view's span, or else the whole capture open open the view series a series name, such as verge: the traces take --series-verge. Without it, or where the page doesn't set that, the stored view's colour on the page's face, or else ink download a link in the summary that downloads the recording and, with annotations, a button that lists its sidecar's files to download (below) shaping shape the recording, as the Open page's converter does: a grip at each row's name moves its channel in time (sideways) or among the rows (up or down), and bars at its data's ends trim it. A move up or down rewrites channels. A group's head has a grip that moves the whole group in time (see groups). A derived channel has no grip or bars: it moves and trims with its first operand. Without it, there are no grips or bars, and no room kept for them Times in attributes are a decimal with a unit (s, ms, us, ns, ps), or a whole number of ticks. A sidecar's stored view applies once its sidecar is in: the view opens on the recording's footer, then shows the stored channels and span. A bundled recording opened with no annotations, channels or window reads its bundle first and draws its first frame in the stored view, so a downloaded file looks as its page showed it. With download, "Download" and, where the view has annotations, "Annotations" sit beside Open, in its look. Download is a link that saves the recording as served, so a bundled file carries its sidecar. Annotations is a button that opens a list over the page, under the button: a link to each file of the sidecar, the hand-written file first, then each file it includes, in its order, each under its own name. Pressed again, or with Escape, the list closes, and the focus going anywhere else closes it too. The list takes the focus at its first link, and Escape gives it back to the button. Each is named for its recording to a screen reader, as Open is: "Download SWD reads", "Download the annotations of SWD reads", and in the list "Download swd.jsonl, from the annotations of SWD reads". Nothing is fetched until a link is clicked, with one exception. The list reads the hand-written file for the files it includes when it first opens, unless the view has read the sidecar already. Where that file doesn't read, the list offers it alone and says why. A browser takes a link's file name only for a file on the page's own site: one on another site downloads under the name its server gives it, or opens in the tab. A local file the page registered downloads under its own name, and lists the sidecar files it was registered with, under theirs. A merge preview, which no file holds, has no links. The reader zooms with Ctrl or Cmd and the wheel, a trackpad pinch, or two fingers. The plain wheel scrolls the page, and the view says how to zoom. Shift with the wheel, a sideways swipe, a drag or the left and right arrow keys move along the capture: an arrow an eighth of the span shown, or half of it with Shift. With the view focused, the up and down arrows or plus and minus zoom in and out. Home and Fit show the whole capture, or all of the channels the view shows, with each analog channel's whole range, and Escape clears the cursors and the selection. A zoom step, and an arrow key's move, eases into place over about 150 ms, and the rows read for where it goes at once. A key pressed during an ease goes on from where the last one was going, and the view eases there from where it is drawn, so a held arrow key glides. A reader who prefers reduced motion sees each step jump there. So does any reader while the view's last three draws each took longer than a frame at 60 Hz, and an ease under way then ends. A drag, a swipe and the wheel move the view at once, and so do Home, Fit and stepping to an annotation. A window the page sets ends an ease there, unless it is the window the ease is going to. Over an analog row's scale, Ctrl or Cmd with the wheel, or two fingers, zoom its values about the pointer instead, a drag moves them, and a double click fits them to the values in view. A scale takes the focus: up and down move it, plus and minus zoom it, Enter fits it and Home shows its whole range. Once a row's values are zoomed in, a drag over its traces with a mouse or a pen moves them too, as well as along the capture. An analog row's whole range is the least and greatest value in its channel's coarsest overview, which are those of all its samples; the row reads that overview first. The plot draws nothing until every analog row's overview has landed, come back empty or failed, so the names column, which the scales' labels widen, is in place from the first frame. When the channels shown change, it keeps its last frame until the new rows' overviews are in. A channel with no overview, as in a merge preview whose recording's ticks don't fall on whole merged ticks, shows its name alone, with no scale, until the view has read all of it; its range then widens the names column. A mouse over a row reads it at the pointer. An analog channel gives the value of the sample there in a label, or the smallest and largest value where one pixel covers several samples. On a digital channel, two spans mark the pulse there: one between its edges for its width, and one over its period to the next edge the same way. A label under the pulse gives its duty, its frequency and 1/width, the width's reciprocal as a rate (one UART bit's gives the baud rate). The width and the period sit on their spans once the row is tall enough for them. Until then the label gives them too, with the pulse's level. A pulse's edges can lie far past what the row has read, as on a quiet line zoomed in close. Once the pointer rests, the view finds them through the overview and reads just those. Moving within the pulse lets the search go on, and once found, the pulse reads at once anywhere in it. Where one pixel holds several edges, the label asks for a closer look. The label keeps to the edge of the rows away from the row it reads, so it never covers the wave there. In a plot too short for it, it runs past the plot's edge. Each row's lower edge, in the names column, is a handle that sets the row's height. Drag it, or focus it and press the up and down arrows (Shift for bigger steps). Home and End give the row its least and greatest height, and Enter or a double click its default. The view grows and shrinks with its rows. Another recording starts every row at its default height. A click places cursor A, and the next click cursor B; with the view focused, Enter places them at the middle of the view. A click's cursor snaps to an edge within 6 pixels on the row clicked. The readout gives both times, the interval between them, and each analog channel's value at each. That value is the last sample at or before the cursor, to the digit one code step carries. It also gives each digital channel's pulse at cursor A, with the figures the pointer gives. A drag along the time axis selects a span. The readout gives its length and each channel's edges in it. For one channel it gives the periods' count, minimum, median and maximum, and the running clock. The running clock is the mean of the periods inside Tukey's fences, as the sidecar's measures define it: it keeps a clock's jitter and quantisation, and drops pauses. The figures come from a count of each distinct period, so their memory grows with how many different periods the span holds, not with how many periods. Past 2,097,152 distinct periods, far more than a clock's, the count, minimum and maximum stay exact, the median is null (the readout shows a dash in its place), and the running clock is the mean of every period, the pauses included. The note says so. tickwave-select's periods carries the same figures. A menu beside the zoom buttons steps through one kind of annotation, "3 of 16". It starts with the kind of the annotation the view opened at, else the kind of the sidecar's first annotation. Clicking an annotation's label shows its span. An annotation's paint draws its channels over its span in its role's look (ANNOTATIONS.md, "Roles"). Between the zoom buttons and the menu, a key lists every role the sidecar declares, in its order: each its label and a short line drawn as the role's lines are. It is the recording's key, not the window's: it changes when the roles or the page's colours do, not as the reader moves. It keeps to one line, cut where the toolbar runs out of room. Method or property Does show(id, span?) opens the view at an annotation, over span ({start, end} in ticks) if one is given. Resolves once it has drawn reveal(id, span?) show(id, span), then brings the view into sight and puts the focus on its plot, as a reference, an inset or a chart's point does focus() puts the focus on the plot, or on the Open button while the view is closed setWindow(start, end) shows a span: ticks, or times such as "317.8 ms". Called before the footer arrives, it shows the span once it has settled() resolves once the view has drawn everything it shows tickAt(clientX) the tick under a point in the window, or null before the view has drawn open whether the view is open; setting it opens or closes it window where the view is going, {start, end} in ticks: the span shown, or while a zoom step eases, the span it eases to cursors cursors A and B, {a, b} in ticks; null where one is not placed selection the selected span, {start, end} in ticks, or null shaping the attribute, as a boolean shape each channel's shape, by its name: offset, the ticks it is moved by, and keep, the part of its own data kept ({from, to} in its ticks before the move), or null for all of it. A group's alignment is not in the offset. Setting it moves and trims the channels it names. Nothing changes the recording groups channels that belong together, such as the recordings of a merge: [{name, channels}], the channels by name. Each group's rows sit under a head row with its name. While the view shapes, a channel's grip moves its row only among its own group's rows aligns each group's alignment, by its name: the ticks all its channels are moved by, later when positive, on top of each channel's own offset. Setting it moves the groups it names annotationsText the sidecar's hand-written file as text, in place of the file at annotations, whose includes it still reads. The view redraws the annotations and keeps its place, cursors and selection. While it is set, the annotation lane shows even with nothing in it, so the first annotation added moves nothing. Null goes back to the file summary the recording's own title and facts, the facts as one line, and matches: whether the text the page slotted matches them. Null until the footer is in, and any stored view the facts wait on (above) Event When, and its detail tickwave-open the view opens: {src} tickwave-window the span shown changes: {start, end} tickwave-select a span is selected: its start, end, duration, edges by channel, and periods for the measured channel tickwave-cursor a cursor is placed or cleared: {a, b} in ticks, and {aTime, bTime}, each a time at the recording's resolution as text; null where a cursor is not placed tickwave-annotation an annotation's label is clicked: {id} tickwave-shape the reader moves, trims or reorders a channel, or moves a group: {shape, aligns, channels, change, channel}: the whole shape and aligns, the rows' names in order, what changed ("move", "trim", "order" or "align"), and the channel's name, or group and its name for "align" tickwave-ready the view has first drawn: {height} tickwave-summary the view has the footer, and any stored view the facts wait on, and has compared the page's title and facts with it: the summary. Again if the page slots other text tickwave-error something failed: {message, error}. The view also shows it, and logs it to the console

One annotation's span, magnified, with the annotation's label and text above it. The annotations inside the span show as notes, and an annotation's paint draws a line in its role's look where the role drives it. An inset sweeps in from the left when it appears. Shown again within 800 ms of hiding, it doesn't sweep again. A reader who prefers reduced motion sees it drawn at once. Attribute Means src, annotations, channels, series as for <tickwave-view> annotation the annotation to show, by id. Set it to switch pad room either side of the span: a share of it ("10%", 6% by default) or a time scale a fixed time scale, such as "50 ns/px", so insets side by side compare sweep off to draw at once for the id of a <tickwave-view> to open at a note href a page to open the recording on at a note, such as tickwave's Open page An annotation's measure puts a reading under the trace, taken from the channel's own edges: rate or period: the running clock over the span. The note says how many periods it used, such as "mean of 31 of 32 periods". duration: the time from the channel's first edge in the span to its last. A reading shows only the digits its ticks support. The key to the roles' lines sits on a line of its own, under the reading: the roles painted within the annotation's span on the inset's channels, in the order the sidecar declares them, each its label and a short line in its look. A reader can point at the inset. Pointing at a note lights its span, and the line under the trace gives the note's label, its length and who drives it, in place of the measure. That names a note too narrow to label. Pointing at a trace reads the pulse there, as the view's label does: its level and width, where it starts in the span, then its period, frequency and duty, as many of them as fit on the line. On an analog channel it reads the value. Moving away puts the measure back. A reader can zoom in within the inset's span, as close as the view goes. Ctrl or Cmd with the wheel, a trackpad pinch, or two fingers zoom it. Zoomed in, a drag with the mouse or a finger moves along the span, as do Shift with the wheel and a sideways swipe. A drag opens nothing. The inset zooms out as far as its span and moves no further than its ends. A zoom step eases as the view's does. Where one pixel holds several edges, the line says how to zoom in. Shown again after 800 ms, or at another annotation, the inset shows its whole span. The inset is one Tab stop, named by its label. The up and down arrow keys zoom in and out, about the lit note or else the middle. The left and right arrows move along the span. Shift with left or right steps through the notes, and a screen reader says each. Zoomed in, the span moves to take in the note stepped to. Escape lights none. On a touch screen, a tap lights a note or reads a pulse. With for or href, the inset opens the recording at a note. A click on a note, Enter on the note the keys lit, or a second tap on a lit note opens it there. A click elsewhere on the plot opens it at the inset's own annotation. Zoomed in, the recording opens over the span the inset shows. for opens a view on the page, and wins where it names one. Otherwise href makes the inset a link to that page: tickwave's Open page, or any page that reads the same parameters. The inset sets src, annotations and annotation in the page's query, and window while zoomed in: the span shown, in whole ticks. It keeps the page's other parameters. While the whole span shows, it drops any window the address had. A recording on the same site goes in by its path, and another site's whole. As a link, the inset opens a new tab on a middle click or a Ctrl or Cmd click, and shows its address on hover. Such an inset marks where it opens, with a small "Opens here" over the plot that moves nothing. It sits on the note lit by the pointer, a tap or the keys. With the keys' focus on the inset and no note lit, it sits at the start of the span shown, where Enter opens. An inset the pointer passes through, as in a chart's popover, where pointer-events is none, does none of this. Inside a popover the inset is no Tab stop, and the element that opened it keeps the focus. A reference passes its arrow keys to arrowKey(event), which answers them as the inset's own and says whether it did. It reads the lit note from lit and the zoomed span from zoomed only while its popover is open, and lights none with clear() as the popover closes. An inset takes its final height once its recording's footer and sidecar are in. The line under the trace is held from then, where the annotation asks for a measure or a reader can point at the inset, so neither the data's arrival nor the pointer moves anything below it. Before then it has no label and no rows to size by. A page that wants nothing to move at all gives the inset its height, as tickwave's main page does for the figure beside its name. settled() and the tickwave-ready event ({annotation, height}) work as on the view, so a page can lay itself out around an inset's final height. sweeping says whether the sweep is playing. window gives the span shown, {start, end} in ticks, and zoomed the span the reader has zoomed to, or null while the whole span shows, as it does again when the inset is shown after 800 ms hidden. While a zoom step eases, window gives the span drawn on the way and zoomed where it is going.

A phrase that cites an annotation. Pointing at it, or reaching it with Tab, opens an inset in a popover beside the text, so nothing on the page moves. The pointer can move into the popover to read the inset, and has 300 ms to cross between the text and the popover. Moving the pointer or the focus away, or Escape, closes the popover. With the focus on the reference, the arrow keys work the inset as they do an inset with the focus. A click, Enter or Space opens its view at the note the pointer or the keys lit, or else at the annotation, and over the span the reader zoomed the popover to. With the popover closed, as after Escape, the view opens at the annotation's own span. A screen reader cannot reach into the drawn inset, so the annotation's label and text describe the reference itself. Attribute Means annotation the annotation it cites for the id of a <tickwave-view> to share a recording with. The reference takes its src, annotations, channels and series src, annotations, series the recording, sidecar and series, for a reference without a view A reference fetches nothing until it scrolls into view. Then it fetches the recording's footer and the sidecar, and the inset fetches the data when it opens.

Measurements against a setting, such as throughput against the clock asked for: a line through each series' points. It is its own module, tickwave-chart.js, and loads nothing else: The chart draws SVG into its own children, not a shadow root, and writes its colours as attributes. So Firefox's reader view, and a page without its CSS, still show the figure. Its caption names it, and the table it names describes it. A reader picks a setting by pointing at it, tapping it or stepping to it with the arrow keys, and picks a series from the legend or a line's end label. A point can name a recording and one of its annotations. Pointing at it opens an inset of that annotation, and a click opens the page's view of the recording there. Only then does the chart load tickwave.js, from beside itself. CHARTS.md, at the repository's root, specifies the data format, tickwave-chart/1, and every attribute, property and event. tickwave.css reserves a chart's room before the module defines it, from --tickwave-chart-height and --tickwave-chart-readout-lines, as it lays out a closed view. Besides the properties below, the chart reads the line patterns (--dash-second-build, --dash-reference, --dash-capture-second, --dash-misread), --capture-width, --capture-opacity and --fault-ink.

The elements draw in the page's own colours and fonts. They read the page's CSS custom properties and fall back to system colours on a page without them: Property Draws --ink, --ink-2 text, traces, cursors; secondary text --page, --surface, --raised the backgrounds under the elements and their controls --hair, --rule dividers; control outlines --wash what the pointer is on --attention-ink a notice of a problem --series-<name> the traces, with series="<name>". Where the page doesn't set it, the recording's stored colour --tickwave-role-<name> the lines paint role <name> draws, over the colour its declaration gives (ANNOTATIONS.md, "Roles") --tickwave-role-<name>-weight CSS pixels the role's lines add to the line weight, from 0 to 4, with or without px --tickwave-role-<name>-dash the role's dash and gap lengths, in line widths, as its declaration gives them: numbers apart by spaces or commas, in pairs, together at least 1. none draws a dashed role solid --tickwave-line-weight the traces' lines in a view and an inset: an analog trace, and a digital row's levels and edges. A number of CSS pixels, with or without px; 1.5 where it is unset or not a positive number. A role's weight adds to it. Rules, axes, the selection and markers stay a pixel wide. The chart doesn't read it --font-text, --font-figures labels; the readouts' figures A digital row reads at most 2,097,152 edges for a view, the view's and a view's width either side. Where the overview it holds can't rule more out, it counts them from the recording's index first. Where those hold more, as a burst far busier than the rest of a long capture can, the row draws its finest overview level, each bucket across the columns it spans, until the view narrows enough. While a zoom's finer data loads, a row draws the coarser data it has. Where that data shows a change it cannot yet place, the row draws it in the trace's colour, faded. A read still going after 5 s puts "Still loading" in the element's notice until it lands. A read that fails puts "Data did not load" there, with the cause, and the stretch stays faded. The row asks again when the view next redraws, 3 s or more later, and the notice goes once the read lands. Each field of a role's look comes from the page's property where it sets one, then from the role's declaration. A colour neither gives comes from the role's place in the order of declarations: the first role in the trace's colour, the rest in ink. A dash neither gives is a solid line. A role's value that doesn't read, such as a weight of 5, is left to the declaration. The elements follow a change of face as it happens: a data-face, a class or a style on <html> that changes the tokens, or the system's preference. A change there that leaves the tokens alone, such as a header marking the page scrolled, redraws nothing. A declared colour takes the face's: the day colour while the page is lighter than its ink, the night colour while it is darker. The elements take a new face in the frame after it changes. A view's and an inset's panels and text follow the page's CSS, and their canvas redraws in that frame. A chart's colours follow the page's CSS without a redraw. Each element exposes its pieces to ::part(). On the view: summary, title, facts, open-button (Open, or Close while the view is open), download-button (Download and Annotations), annotations-download-button (Annotations), annotations-download-list (the list it opens), annotations-download-link (each link in the list), annotations-download-note (why the list holds the hand-written file alone), viewer, toolbar, key, plot, hint, reading (the label at the pointer), row-handle, readout, steps, notice and button (each button, and the Download link). Inside facts, each fact is a fact and also fact-length, fact-channels or fact-size, with a fact-separator ("; ") between two. On the inset: inset, label, text, frame, canvas, plot (over the canvas, what the pointer and the keys reach), foot, measure, reading (what the pointer or the keys lit), key and notice. On the reference: popover. A part an element hides stays hidden, whatever display a page's rule gives it. A page's slotted spans sit inside title and facts, and take the page's own rules. A page sets the view's summary through these properties, set on the view or above it. tickwave.css reads them too, which ::part() cannot reach, so a view styled this way keeps its height when it is defined: Property Sets Without it --tickwave-summary-padding the summary's padding 8px 10px 8px 14px --tickwave-summary-gap the gap between its rows, and between the text and the button 2px 12px --tickwave-summary-border-width its border's widths 1px --tickwave-summary-border-color its border's colour var(--hair) --tickwave-summary-background its background var(--surface) --tickwave-summary-radius its corners' radius 10px --tickwave-title-size the title's font size the view's --tickwave-facts-size the facts' font size 13px --tickwave-open-button-size the Open button's font size 13px --tickwave-open-button-padding its padding 3px 9px --tickwave-open-button-height its least height 26px The title and the facts take the view's font-size and line-height. The title is weight 600 and breaks anywhere it must; a page that changes that, or the facts' colour, styles its own spans. Nothing moves under the reader. A readout's figures are tabular, and an inset's reading sets a pulse's level as wide as "high" either way, so what follows it holds still as the pointer crosses edges. A line of a readout, or of an inset's foot, is as tall from the first as once its figures come: a selection's counts and periods show "…" in the figures' font, and the periods' menu, while they are worked out. The label at a view's pointer keeps off the row it reads. An inset takes its final height once its footer and sidecar are in, so the data arriving moves nothing below it. A control stays where the reader pressed it. One that opens or switches something undoes it when pressed again: a view's Open button reads Close while the view is open, and is as wide either way.

<tickwave-chart> draws measurements against a setting, such as throughput against the clock asked for. This document specifies the element and its data, tickwave-chart/1. Status: draft, with the recording format.

Each series is a line through its points. A point can name the wire recording behind it: pointing at the point opens an inset of that recording, as <tickwave-ref> does for a phrase in the text. The x values are a short list of settings, the same for every series. The y values are measurements. A chart is not a capture: it has no time axis, no zoom and no decoder.

tickwave-chart.js is its own module. It is published beside tickwave.js in each version's directory (/tickwave/v<semver>/), so one version covers every file: <script type="module" src="tickwave-chart.js"></script> A page without charts never loads it. A chart loads nothing else until a reader points at a point that names a recording. Then it imports tickwave.js from beside itself, and the inset loads the worker and the WASM module as it does on any page. A page that has already loaded the elements keeps its own. A chart in the page's markup takes no room until the module defines it, and its data comes after that. To keep the page still through both, link tickwave.css, published beside the modules, and state the chart's room in CSS: <link rel="stylesheet" href="tickwave.css"> <style> #throughput { --tickwave-chart-height: 250px; --tickwave-chart-readout-lines: 3; } </style> <tickwave-chart id="throughput" src="throughput.chart.json" readout="below"></tickwave-chart> tickwave.css reserves the plot's height and, for a readout below, its lines, until the chart is defined. The chart then holds the same room until its data arrives. A legend above the plot comes with the data, since its rows depend on the series and the width.

The chart draws SVG into its own children, not into a shadow root. Firefox's reader view keeps an element's SVG children and drops any shadow root, clonable or not (Firefox 160). The SVG reads the same in reader view, in a feed, or on a page without its CSS: Data colours come from the page's tokens when the chart draws, and go into the SVG as presentation attributes. Each also has a style that refers to its token, so where the page's CSS applies, the colours follow the face without a redraw. Reader view clears the style and keeps the attributes. Text, grid, axes and neutral marks are currentColor. Fonts are presentation attributes, since reader view's sanitizer clears style. Nothing refers to an id (url(#id)), since reader view sets a <base>. So the entry sweep cuts the lines where it has reached, rather than clipping them. The chart draws at its box's width in CSS pixels, not into a fixed viewBox that scales. Text stays at its CSS size at any width, and the chart redraws when its box changes width. d3-scale places the points on both axes. The x axis labels the settings themselves, from x.values. It leaves out a label that would sit within 22 px of the one before it: a tick at a value nobody measured would mislead. The y axis takes d3's ticks, in steps of 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten, unless the data fixes them. The plot's left margin makes room for the widest y label and for the unit above them.

A chart reads one JSON object, from a URL (src) or from the page (data). Every value is a decimal string, as whatever measured it wrote it. "81.0" keeps its last digit, where a JSON number would lose it. A readout shows a value with exactly the digits it came with, and groups the whole part's thousands with commas: "1238.6" reads "1,238.6". The landing page's Figure 1, cut to three clocks: { "format": "tickwave-chart/1", "source": "mculink-bench results/throughput/2026-11-04: SWD, probe-rs 4 KiB writes, the median of two runs", "x": { "name": "SWD clock asked for", "unit": "MHz", "scale": "log", "values": ["20", "30", "50"] }, "y": { "name": "4 KiB writes", "unit": "KiB/s", "scale": "linear", "max": "2500", "step": "500" }, "series": [ { "id": "clang", "name": "Verge, Clang build", "short": "Verge", "colour": "verge", "pattern": "solid", "marker": "circle", "points": [{ "value": "1238.6" }, { "value": "1779.8" }, { "value": "2257.8" }] }, { "id": "stock", "name": "NXP's firmware V3.174", "short": "NXP", "colour": "nxp", "pattern": "solid", "marker": "circle", "points": [ { "value": "666.7" }, { "failed": true }, { "partial": { "failed": 1, "of": 2, "value": "744.6" }, "verdict": "wrong" } ] } ], "limits": [{ "x": "20", "series": "stock", "label": "NXP's firmware reads right up to 20 MHz" }] }

Every series has one point for each x.min, x.max the axis' ends, where it reaches past the first and last settings: "0.8" and "62.5" keep points at 1 and 50 MHz off the plot's edges x.name, x.unit, y.name, y.unit the axes' names. A unit is written once, at its axis x.scale, y.scale linear or log y.max, y.step a fixed top and tick step. Without them, the chart picks both from the data reference "y=x" draws the diagonal, named "as asked" in the legend

Field Means id names the series in attributes, events and other charts: letters, digits, ., _ and - name in the legend and in a readout below the plot short in the end label, a fail mark ("GCC failed"), a tooltip readout, and a readout below where name does not fit colour a series token: verge draws in --series-verge pattern solid, second-build, reference or capture-second: the design system's line patterns marker circle, square, diamond, triangle-up or triangle-down capture a run under energy capture: the line takes --capture-width and --capture-opacity hidden drawn only once the page shows it fails "mark": a failure takes a mark at the axis ("GCC failed"). Without it, a failure shows only as the break in the line and in the readout

A point is null where the series has no figure and nothing to say about it. A line joins only neighbouring settings that both have a value, and breaks at any other. A segment across a setting would read as a figure there, whether the run failed, partly failed or never happened. The point has no value. The line breaks, a fail mark shows if the series marks its failures, and the readout gives this figure range ["1230.1", "1247.0"]: the spread across runs, in the readout ring a ring around the point note a few words the readout adds after the figure: "18.4 MHz, the read failed partway" evidence { "recording": "...", "annotations": "...", "annotation": "..." }: the recording, its sidecar, and the annotation that shows this point. URLs are relative to the chart's file, or to the page for data set through data. A failed or partial point's recording opens from its fail mark, so only in a series that marks its failures
A vertical line at an x, dashed, with its label in the legend. With series, the line grows from that series' point during the entry sweep.

Attribute Means src the chart's data show the series to draw, by id. Without it, every series not hidden selected an x selected from the start. With it, a selection stays until another replaces it. Without it, the selection follows the pointer and clears group charts with the same group share their selected x highlight points to ring, as series@x, and limits to strengthen the limit lines as their legend entry does: "clang@50 stock@20 limits". A claim in the prose sets it readout tooltip, beside the selected x, or below, a row under the plot legend above draws a legend over the plot. Without it, the page has its own key end-labels names each line at its last point, with its short. Labels that would overlap move apart, and the plot leaves room for the widest table the id of the page's table that gives the chart as text height the plot's height in CSS pixels. --tickwave-chart-height wins over it sweep off draws at once

Property or method Does data the chart's data as an object. Setting it redraws: a page that slices a larger table sets each slice here. The reader's picked x stays picked where the new data has it. Reading it gives the parsed data, not the object set, so a page that skips unchanged data keeps track of what it set pick(x, series) selects an x, a series or both, as a reader's pick does, and moves the group with it. It fires no event. pick() clears settled() resolves once the chart has drawn, its sweep included reserved the room the chart took at its first layout with data, {height, lines, matches}: the plot's height in CSS pixels, the readout's lines (null for a tooltip), and whether the page's properties reserved it. Null before Event When, and its detail tickwave-pick the reader picks an x or a series: {x, series}, either null when cleared tickwave-evidence the reader opens a point's recording: {x, series, recording, annotations, annotation}, the URLs absolute. Cancelable (see Evidence) tickwave-reserved the chart has laid out its first data and compared its room with the page's properties: the reserved value tickwave-ready the chart has first drawn: {height} tickwave-error the data did not load or does not parse: {message, error}

A reader picks an x by pointing at the plot or tapping it. The nearest x is picked: each x owns the band between the midpoints to its neighbours. The chart takes focus, and the arrow keys step through the x values. Escape clears, and so does a tap outside the chart. A mouse leaving the plot clears, and a finger lifting does not. With selected, nothing clears. A reader picks a series from the legend or from its end label. The other series fade to 20 %. A page picks one with pick, for a table column or a key. The readout gives the picked x and each shown series' figure there, with the series' swatch: its line and marker as drawn. A figure takes its range in brackets, its partial runs, its note and its verdict, such as "failed in 1 of 2 runs (744.6 KiB/s in the other), reads wrong". As a tooltip, the readout sits beside the picked x, or to its left near the plot's right edge. It sits at the plot's top, or lower where that hides less of the lines. A long line wraps. A readout below the plot holds a line for the x and one for each shown series, whether or not an x is picked, so a pick moves nothing under it. Before the data, it holds the lines --tickwave-chart-readout-lines states, or else those for the series show names. Each line stays one line. A series whose name does not fit beside its figures, at the chart's width, takes its short for every x, and a name that still does not fit ends in an ellipsis. A figure is never cut. The full name stays in the line's text for a screen reader, and shows when the pointer rests on it. On a chart too narrow for some setting's readout to fit beside it, as on a phone, the tooltip floats off the chart for every setting. It sits below the chart at the picked x, or above it where the window has no room below. There it covers the page around the chart, and none of the chart.

A point that names a recording behaves as <tickwave-ref> does. An inset of its annotation opens in a popover when a mouse rests within 12 px of the point for 150 ms, when a finger taps it, or when the keys reach its setting. The popover opens below the chart, or above it when there is no room below, across the point's x. Nothing on the page moves, and the popover covers none of the chart, nor a floating readout: the picked x's rule joins it to the point.
