It compresses blocks at the level it is given, and overview blocks at zstd level 3, whatever that level is. Annotation parts are compressed at the level it is given, strips and the annotation bundle at the finish. By default the compression of every other frame is spread over the calls after its record is made, on the caller's thread: a frame is cut into slices of 8 KiB of decoded bytes from its start, and while any frame is pending, every call, take_output included, compresses the next slice, and the slices after it while they fit in 8 KiB together, so no call does much work however large a block is. Each slice ends a zstd block inside the frame, so the frame's bytes depend on the data, the level and the slice, never on how the calls fall. Its records leave in file order: a record waits behind the frames before it, so a flush's known-through record leaves only after the bytes of that flush's blocks. A closed block reaches the output within one call for each slice still to compress of the frames up to and including its own. A ready-made option compresses on other threads instead, channels in parallel, and gives the same bytes. finish compresses whatever is still pending. Memory. It holds each channel's open block, at most 4 MiB, each table's open pages at each depth (at most 4,096 entries each) and the top index's entries, each overview level's open block and open run with their sums, each derived channel's waiting samples, at most 4 MiB, each generator's lines since its last annotation part, under 64 KiB and one line, each channel's gaps whose blocks are still open, at most 4 MiB of them, the frames waiting for compression, and the content id's running digests. Each of those is bounded whatever the recording's length, so a month-long recording holds a few open pages of index, not every block's row, gap or annotation. Some fill slowly: a coarse level's open block over days, a directory's open page over months, so the writer's memory rises toward that bound for a long while. Gaps and runs. It writes a run's record with the run's first sample, so it leaves out no run. It hashes a gap, and adds it to its list's open page, once the channel's block that holds the gap's to closes. It refuses a gap that would leave more than 4 MiB of gaps waiting, at 17 bytes each, as it refuses an item past its limit; the producer then promises or flushes. At the finish it hashes a gap still waiting unless the channel's end leaves it out, and refuses an end that would leave out a gap it has hashed. Annotations. It writes a generator's annotation part once that generator's lines since its last part reach 64 KiB, after the record whose line takes them there. Before a line that would take them past 4 MiB, it writes the lines it holds as a part first. At the finish it writes each generator's rest, then the bundle record, whose hand-written file includes the generator files. It doesn't check a generator's ids for duplicates. Nothing it does at the finish reads back what it wrote.

A reader reads the file's last 32 KiB first: over HTTP with Range: bytes=-32768, which a server answers with the whole file when it is shorter. It reads the trailer, and fetches the rest of the footer if the footer starts before those bytes. It parses the footer once, and decompresses the strips of the channels it shows: that is a first draw. For a span of a channel it then picks a level by the width of a column: the coarsest of the channel's levels whose bucket is no wider than a column, or the channel's items where even its finest is wider. It fetches that table's pages through the top index, directory pages first where the table has them, then the overview blocks or blocks the span covers, as the rows place them, and those either side of the span, so a pan seldom waits. It decodes each block once for a view, whatever channels the view takes from it. It checks each length a row or a directory entry states against the limits before it fetches (see Limits). For annotations it reads the bundle record and the annotation parts table's rows, and fetches the parts whose span meets the view, as it fetches blocks. A reader that only draws the data may leave annotations until after the first draw.

A channel is unavailable to a reader when its requires names a feature the reader doesn't know, its kind or its codec is one it doesn't know, or, for a derived channel, its op is one it doesn't know or an operand is unavailable. The reader still opens the recording. It keeps the channel's place and name, so every other channel keeps its number, and shows the channel as unavailable rather than leaving it out. It skips the channel's blocks, overview and strip; the top index still says where they are, so it reads past them. A later version can raise a limit for its own channels, so a reader holds an unavailable channel to the format's layout alone, not to the limits: its rows and lists to the shape and count of each page, row and entry, not to the values in them; its strip to the footer's bounds, not to a strip's size; and, reading in order, its block and overview block records to their framing alone, at any length a record holds, hashing and skipping each as it does a record of a kind from 128 up. It fetches and decodes none of the frames they place. It leaves out every annotation that names an unavailable channel in channels or measure, even one that names other channels too, and says which annotations it left out and why. An annotation whose channels is absent or empty names no channel by name, and stays. A reader holds the rest of an unavailable channel's entry, where its kind is one it knows, to this version's rules all the same, its mapping into 0..length included (see Header). So a feature that changes how a source's ticks map to the axis goes in the requires of every channel of that source, and states an origin and a stretch that place each channel's kept span and end inside the axis by this version's rule too. A full check, which compares every item with what the file states, can't check a channel it can't read, so it refuses a recording that has one and says which.

A reader takes the records from the start. Each block record carries its channel, its span and its word, so the reader decodes a channel's blocks without the footer, and each known-through record extends every channel to its tick. It may skip pages, and annotation parts that cover records, whose contents follow from the records it reads; tickwave's reader checks each against them instead, and refuses one that differs by a byte from what the records before it give. A part that stands alone, and the annotation bundle, follow from no record: the bundle holds the hand-written file and each generator file's first line. The reader refuses each record that breaks a rule this document gives for records in order. It stops at the first record that runs past the end of the file, whose n passes its kind's limit, or whose check does not match, and keeps every record before it. A file that stops before its trailer is cut off, not finished: a full check refuses it, and repair can finish it. A file that ends with a trailer whose footer ends where the trailer starts is finished; if its records stop before that footer, it is damaged, not cut off. A reader with random access may still read it, and repair and re-cutting refuse it, since finishing it again would drop what follows the stop. After the footer record come exactly the trailer's 24 bytes. A viewer reading a file that is still being written meets a last record cut off where the writer has got to. It reads that record again once the file grows. The declaration fixes each channel's finest level, so the viewer extends each channel's levels bucket by bucket as its blocks and the known-through records arrive, and adds a coarser level once the length needs one.

A cut-off file is repaired by appending what a finished file has after its last good record: Take the records up to the first bad one. Refuse a file with no declaration, or with no block, no known-through record and no annotation record. Where they hold a known-through record, cut the file just after the latest one: every channel is then known to its tick, and none holds more. Keep the annotation records that came after it, to write again after the cut. An annotation part after the cut that covers records goes, and its lines come back from the records; one that stands alone is kept, to write again. Note, too, each gap record after the cut whose from maps before the known-through tick: a loss the recorder had begun to report then ends its channel at that from (step 4), rather than being lost with the cut. It is written again only where its to maps at or past the length (step 3), as a gap the header leaves out (see Gap and run records); otherwise only its from stays. A record only a finish writes goes wherever it lies, since a file cut there was cut inside its finish and step 7 writes it again: a table's last page, one of fewer than 4,096 entries, and the annotation bundle. Where they hold none, each channel keeps its blocks to its last whole one, except that a derived channel's operands keep only the samples both hold: cut the file just after the last record at which every derived channel's operands hold as many samples, and keep the annotation records and parts after the cut as above. The length is the later of that known-through tick (or, with none, the latest end of any kept block, 0 with no block) and one past the latest start among the annotations kept, so what a recorder marked after its last data survives, and a recording of marks alone too. Each channel whose last kept block ends before the length gets an empty block from there, or from tick 0, to the length. Every digital channel's end is the source tick at the latest known-through tick, or, with none, at its own last kept block's end, or its start with no block, or the from of a gap noted in step 2 where that comes sooner. A file that can be repaired states no kept span, so its one source maps by T = k + origin, and that tick is the axis tick minus origin. No analog channel states a loss after its last sample. Count each channel's edges and samples from its blocks' words, and take its gaps and runs from their records. Compute each channel's overview and the content id from the kept blocks' items, decoding each block once. Keep the overview blocks and pages already written that the kept blocks give, and write the rest, the open runs included. Refuse a file whose overview blocks or pages differ from the ones its content gives. Each channel's levels are compared on their own, in order of k, whatever order the records of different channels and levels came in. Write the records kept in step 2 after the cut, in the order they came. Before a part that stands alone, write a part of the lines of its generator's records written again before it, so that it still stands alone. Then write what a writer's finish writes. For each generator, in the order of its first annotation, that is parts of the lines of its records after its last kept part, each within the limits. A record a kept part covers is not written into another part. Then come every table's last pages, the annotation bundle, the footer and the trailer. A repaired file holds what a writer that had finished right after the records repair keeps, with the same length, would have written, and so has its content id. A gap record among the records step 2 keeps is not written again but stays where it lies. Where one reaches its channel's end (step 4) while its to maps before the length (step 3), the header can't leave the gap out (see Gap and run records), and repair can't take the record out of what it keeps. Such a file is not repaired, but re-cut (see Re-cutting): the copy then holds the same content without the record. So is a file with an auxiliary record among the records step 2 keeps, since a tool that writes a recording again drops every one (see Preamble). A file whose channels state kept, because a channel is moved or cut, the recording merges several sources, or its source states a stretch other than 1, is not repaired. Its declaration states each channel's kept span before any data, to the end of the whole capture, so a footer at an earlier tick would contradict it. Such a file is made again from its sources instead.

A file whose blocks a recorder closed early, at flushes, can be written again with blocks of the usual size, and a repaired file too. A re-cutter reads the records in order and writes the same declaration, then every channel's items, and the gaps and runs its header lists, in the same order, and finishes with the same length, ends, losses, extras and annotations. It writes the annotations as parts that stand alone, with no annotation records (see Annotations). It may give the channels other overview shifts than the input declares, such as the ones the rule gives each channel's own items; a finished input's header says enough to work them out. It computes the overview again. The new file has the same content id. A cut-off file re-cuts as repair would finish it, and so does one repair refuses for a gap record it keeps: a re-cutter leaves out every gap record that reaches its channel's end while its to maps before the length, wherever it lies, and ends the channel at the earliest such gap's from.

Annotations mark spans and points on a recording: a transfer, an acknowledge, a misread, a stretched clock period. They live beside the recording in text files, so they diff, take hand edits, and regenerate without touching the capture. Page text cites an annotation by its id. Status: draft, with the recording format.

A recording rec.tickwave has one hand-written TOML file, rec.annotations.toml. A program that generates annotations, such as a protocol decoder, writes its own JSON Lines file, which the TOML file includes: rec.wire_swd.jsonl. An included file sits beside the hand-written one and is named on its own, without a directory. A generator rewrites its file whole on each run. It may start the hand-written file when there is none, and never writes it after that. From then on only tickwave's editor edits it, and it keeps the file's comments, order and layout, so a rerun cannot touch a hand edit. A script that re-pins a sidecar to a reconverted recording may rewrite recording_id, and nothing else. A generator runs after the recording is converted. It reads the recording's id from tickwave info --json (header.content_id).

format = "tickwave-annotations/1" recording = "rec.tickwave" # optional; checked against the file name when known recording_id = "blake3:4f2a…" # the recording's content id include = ["rec.wire_swd.jsonl"] # generator files, beside this one [[annotation]] id = "read-ack-check" start = "317.85882 ms" end = "317.85891 ms" channels = ["SWCLK", "SWDIO"] label = "The 12-cycle period before read data" kind = "period" measure = { channel = "SWCLK", what = "rate" } [[annotation]] id = "first-misread" ref = "wire_swd/misread/412093311" label = "NXP's firmware misreads at 25 MHz"

The first line names the generator. Each later line is one annotation. Blank lines are skipped. {"format": "tickwave-annotations/1", "source": "wire_swd", "version": "9f3c2e1", "recording_id": "blake3:4f2a…"} {"id": "misread/412093311", "kind": "misread", "start": 412093311, "end": 412094105, "channels": ["SWDIO"], "label": "parity wrong"} source is the generator's name. It is not empty and holds no whitespace, / or \: tickwave names the generator's file after it, rec.<source>.jsonl, beside the recording. version is optional: the generator's own commit or hash, for provenance. role is optional too: the paint roles the generator's lines paint with, each a table as the hand-written file's [[role]] gives one (below). {"format": "tickwave-annotations/1", "source": "wire_swd", "recording_id": "blake3:4f2a…", "role": [{"name": "probe", "label": "probe drives"}, {"name": "target", "label": "target drives", "weight": 1}]}

Field Meaning id Hand-written: any name without whitespace or /. Generated: the full id is <source>/<id>. start, end Times. end is absent for a point. channels Channel names. Absent or empty means every channel. label Short text shown with the annotation. kind A free word (transfer, misread, stall). Styling and filtering key on it. text Longer text, shown in an inset's caption. paint A role the sidecar declares (below), such as probe: the annotation's channels draw over its span in the role's look. measure {channel, what}: the inset shows a measure taken from the channel's edges inside the span (below). The channel must be digital, and the annotation a span. values Figures the annotation states, by name, each a decimal and its unit (below). ref Hand-written only: the full id of a generated annotation. This one takes its span and channels, and any field it leaves out. A file may hold no other fields, measure's included: a misspelt one is an error, not ignored. A key stated twice in any object of an annotation, its measure and values included, is an error too, whatever the file's version. A later minor version can add fields (see Versions).

A paint role says who drives a line, or anything else a page colours a stretch of a channel by. The sidecar declares each role it paints with: the hand-written file in [[role]] tables, and a generator in its file's first line, as role. [[role]] name = "neither" label = "neither drives" colour = ["#8a8a8a", "#5c5c5c"] dash = [2, 1] Field Meaning name What a paint names. Lower-case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, at most 32 bytes. label What a key and a readout say for the role, at most 200 bytes. The name where it is left out. colour "#rrggbb" for both faces, or a [day, night] pair of them. weight CSS pixels added to the trace's line weight, from 0 to 4. 0 where it is left out. dash The role's dash and gap lengths, in pairs: at most 8 numbers, each from 0 to 64, together at least 1. Each is a number of the role's line widths, its weight included. A solid line where it is left out. A role takes no other field. A file declares at most 64 roles, and so do a sidecar's files between them. A file that declares more is one problem, and its roles past the 64th are not read. A paint names a declared role. The check reports one that names no declared role, once for each name, where it is first used. A reader that shows such a sidecar keeps the annotation, draws its channels as if it painted nothing, and keys nothing for it. Roles keep the order they are declared in: the hand-written file's, then each generator's, in the order include lists the files. One name may be declared in several files, alike: each field is compared once its default is filled in, a label left out being the name, a weight left out 0, and one colour being the pair of it. A colour or a dash left out equals only one left out. A name declared differently in two files is a problem. A name declared alike again keeps the place it first took. A file that declares one name twice is a problem. Each field of a role's look comes from the first of these that gives it: The host: the page's --tickwave-role-<name>, -weight and -dash (web/README.md, "Styling"), or an egui host's Palette::roles. A host's weight or dash outside the bounds a declaration's is held to is left to the declaration, and a host can make a dashed role solid. The role's declaration. For the colour alone, the role's place in the order of declarations: the first role takes the trace's colour, and the rest ink. A role neither gives a dash is solid. A declared colour takes the host's face: its day colour by day, its night colour by night. Where several annotations paint a channel at a tick, the latest in sidecar order draws it. A dash runs on along a painted stretch from where the stretch starts, across the line's edges, and starts again after a gap in the data. The roles travel with the recording when it is bundled, in the hand-written file and the generators' first lines. A recording that a writer finishes bundles each generator's roles in its file's first line. One repaired after it was cut off before it finished keeps none of them: the writer holds them until it finishes. Nor does a recording read from a writer's snapshot as it is written have them.

The hand-written file may store how a view of the recording starts, in a [view] table. A page or a host that says how to show the recording wins over it. [view] channels = ["SWDIO", "SWCLK"] start = "377.09 ms" end = "377.25 ms" colour = ["#d9480f", "#ff8a50"] Field Meaning channels The channels a view shows, in this order. Every channel where it is left out. start, end The span a view shows first: times, as annotations' are. The capture's start and end where they are left out. colour The trace's colour, "#rrggbb" or a [day, night] pair, under the page's series colour. Ink where it is left out. Each channel is the recording's, and named once; channels lists one at least. The span lies in the capture and ends after it starts. The table takes no other field.

measure takes the channel's edges at ticks in [start, end): an edge at end is outside. It shows no more digits than its ticks carry. A span meant to measure from one edge to another starts at the first edge's tick and ends one tick past the last. rate and period: the running clock. Its periods run from one rising edge to the next, so a span needs at least two rising edges. Sort the span's n periods as p[0..n). Take Q1 = p[⌊(n − 1)/4⌋], Q3 = p[⌈3(n − 1)/4⌉], and IQR = Q3 − Q1, but at least one tick. Keep the periods within [Q1 − 1.5 IQR, Q3 + 1.5 IQR]: Tukey's fences. The measure is the mean of the kept periods, as a rate or a period, and the inset says how many it kept ("mean of 31 of 32 periods"). The fences keep a clock's edge jitter and its quantisation, such as 26 and 27 ns for a 26.67 ns clock. They drop pauses, and a long period that occurs in fewer than a quarter of the periods, such as a slow acknowledge check or a stretched cycle. duration: the time from the channel's first edge in the span to its last, of either polarity. A span needs at least two edges.

values holds the figures an annotation states, for a page's charts and tables to read. A decoder that measures a session writes them beside its label: [[annotation]] id = "session-50" ref = "wire_swd/session/377858886" values = { asked = "50 MHz", read_data = "37.5 MHz", write_data = "49.9 MHz" } In a generator's file the same is "values": {"asked": "50 MHz", ...}. A name is lower-case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter. A value is a decimal, then one space and a unit where it has one: a count, such as a marker's number, has none. It is a string, so "81.0 KiB/s" keeps its last digit. tickwave never converts or rounds a value. A page compares units as text, so micro is always µ (U+00B5 MICRO SIGN), as in times, and never the Greek letter mu (U+03BC).

A time is either a whole number of ticks from the capture's start, as a JSON integer (digits with an optional -, no fraction or exponent, so not 12.0), or a string holding a decimal and a unit. The decimal is digits with at most one . among them and at least one digit, such as 12, 12.5, .5 or 12., with an optional - or + before it. The unit is s, ms, us, µs, ns or ps, after the decimal with or without whitespace between, and whitespace around the whole is ignored, whitespace being any character Unicode's White_Space property holds: "12 ms", "12ms" and " 0.012 s " are one time. An exponent, digits grouped with spaces, or a decimal without a unit is an error. A decimal converts to ticks exactly, without floating point, and rounds to the nearest tick, halves away from zero. A time still lies in 0..2^53 ticks once converted.

Page text cites ids, so they must survive a decoder's rerun. A generator derives each id from the recording, not from the run: its kind and start tick, as misread/412093311, not a counter. A hand-written ref gives a generated annotation a name that reads well in prose.

Annotations keep sidecar order: the hand-written file's, in its order, then each included file's, in the order include lists the files, line by line. Order carries meaning: a view steps through the kind of the first annotation unless it was opened at another, so an author lists first an annotation of the kind a page steps through.

tickwave annotations check --json prints the annotations resolved, in sidecar order, and the browser's decoder hands the page the same. Each has its full id, source (the generator's name; null for a hand-written one), start and end in ticks, and the fields above. An alias keeps ref, the full id of the generated annotation it names, so a page can tell the two apart. A reader that leaves out a generated annotation leaves out an alias of it too, and says so: a ref resolves only to an annotation the reader keeps.

tickwave annotations check rec.tickwave rec.annotations.toml reports every problem it finds, then exits non-zero if there was any. A page's build runs it, so a decoder rerun that drops an annotation the prose cites breaks the build instead of the page. It checks that: both files declare format tickwave-annotations/1, or a later minor version of it (see Versions), and their recording_id matches the recording; recording, if given, names the recording's file; every included file is named without a directory, is provided, and every provided file is included; each generator's name is one the rule above allows; ids are unique, hand-written ids hold no /, and every ref names a generated annotation; every channel exists, a point and a span's start lie in 0..length, and a span's end is not before its start and not past length; every measure names a digital channel, or one of a kind this version doesn't know, which may have edges; a known measure; and sits on a span; every value is a decimal, with one space and a unit where it has one, under a name of lower-case letters, digits and _; each role declaration holds to the rules above, no name is declared twice in a file or differently in two, and no file declares more than 64 roles, nor the files between them; every paint names a declared role; a [view] table holds to the rules above.

A file's format names its version: tickwave-annotations/1 is version 1, minor version 0, and tickwave-annotations/1.<n> is minor version n. A minor version adds what a reader of an earlier one can leave out and still read everything else as the file means it: top-level keys of the hand-written file or of a generator's first line, fields of an annotation, of a role, of measure and of the [view] table, and values of measure's what. In a file of a later minor version than it knows, a reader leaves out each such key it doesn't know, and each measure whose what it doesn't know, says which in a note that is not a problem, and keeps the annotation, role or view they were in. In a file of its own minor version or an earlier one, a key it doesn't know is an error, as everywhere else in these files. Any other version is another format, which check refuses. A tool that writes these files again carries what it doesn't know rather than leaving it out. A re-cut and repair carry an annotation's keys and measures they don't know, whatever its file's version, and name them, since a generator's first line, which says its version, may reach them after its annotations do (FORMAT.md, "Annotations"). Repair writes a first line of its own version for a generator whose first line was lost with the cut, so a reader of that version then counts the keys it carried as errors. A merge reads each generator's first line before its lines, and carries what it doesn't know only from a file of a later minor version than its own. Each still leaves out, and names, a line that breaks a rule on a key it knows.

tickwave bundle rec.tickwave rec.annotations.toml -o shared.tickwave checks the sidecar, then writes a copy of the recording with the sidecar's files in it, for a single-file share: the hand-written file and each generator file's first line in its annotation bundle, and each generator file's other lines in annotation parts (FORMAT.md, "Annotations"). The content id stays the same. The roles and the stored view are in the bundle, so a reader has them before it reads any part.

tickwave merge carries each input's generated annotations into the merged recording: the generator files it holds, joined from its annotation bundle and annotation parts, or, where it has none, those its sidecar beside it includes. They are bundled again under the merged recording's id. Each time moves with its input as its input's sources do (FORMAT.md, "Sources"): a time x of the input's lies at the input's move plus floor(x × s × R / R_input) on the merged recording's axis, s the input's stretch and R / R_input the merged rate over the input's, and is written in its ticks. Inputs go in the order given. A generator whose name an earlier input's generator took is renamed <stem>-<name>, where <stem> is the input's file name without its extension, with any whitespace written as _. A second clash takes <stem>-2-<name>, and so on. The full ids of its annotations change with it, and so does the source its file's first line names, so a tool that looks for its own generator's file by name finds only the first input's. An annotation whose times move outside the merged recording is left out: a span that ends at or before its start, or anything that starts at or past its end. A span that reaches over either end is cut there. A line that doesn't read is left out too, and so is one that breaks a rule above for a generator's line. The merge counts each of these. Channel names in channels and measure follow the names the merge gives. A channel the merge leaves out is dropped from channels, and an annotation left with none is left out. A measure on a channel left out is dropped. An annotation without channels, or with an empty list, which meant every channel of its recording, names that input's channels. Each carried generator's file keeps its first line as it was: its version, version, the roles it declares and any other key, but for source, renamed as above, and recording_id, the merged recording's. Two inputs whose generators declare one name differently, or a declaration that breaks a rule above, stop the merge: the merged sidecar would fail its check. A hand-written file's annotations are not carried, since their times are the input's. The merge says how many it left out. Its roles and its stored view are not carried either.
